title: Logic in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain what logic and critical thinking do: check whether the reasons for a claim really support it.
summary: Logic sorts good arguments from bad by asking whether reasons support a claim. Its name comes from Greek logos. Dewey's reflective thought weighs a belief by the grounds behind it.

cards.headline: "The café must be closed. The lights are off." Good reason?
cards.body: Maybe. Or maybe the owner just likes candlelight. You hear reasons like this all day, from friends, from ads and from your own head. This whole skill is about one question: do the reasons really support the claim?

cards.headline: What logic does
cards.body: Logic studies reasoning. Logic has many uses, and the open textbook forall x focuses on this one: evaluating arguments, sorting the good ones from the bad. It adds that logic might even be called the science of what follows from what. So at the café, logic's question isn't "Is it closed?" It's "Do dark windows get you to closed?" Dark windows and an open door can go together.

cards.fact: "Logic" comes from the Greek logos: word, reason.
cards.context: It reached English through Latin logica, from the Greek logike techne, "the reasoning art". The name fits. Logic works on reasons put into words, the kind you can say out loud, write down and then test.

cards.headline: Critical thinking: logic for everyday life
cards.body: In How We Think, published in 1910, the American philosopher John Dewey described reflective thought: careful consideration of any belief in the light of the grounds that support it. The idea of teaching critical thinking goes back to him. His advice for the café? Hold off deciding until you've looked at the grounds.
cards.callout: Dewey: "The essence of critical thinking is suspended judgment."

cards.headline: Logic: introduced
learned: Logic sorts good arguments from bad
"Logic" comes from Greek logos: word, reason
Dewey: weigh a belief by the grounds that support it
Critical thinking starts with suspended judgment

questions.prompt: According to the textbook forall x, what use of logic does it focus on?

options.label: Collecting true facts about the world
options.rationale: Logic checks reasoning; gathering facts is other fields' work.

options.label: Sorting good arguments from bad ones
Helping you win every debate
options.rationale: Logic judges arguments, not who wins.

options.label: Proving that opinions are wrong
options.rationale: It judges arguments, not opinions as such.

questions.explanation: forall x focuses on logic's use in evaluating arguments: sorting the good from the bad.

questions.prompt: John Dewey's "reflective thought" weighs a belief in the light of what?

options.label: How popular the belief is
options.rationale: Popularity isn't a ground Dewey names.

options.label: How strongly you feel it
options.rationale: Feelings aren't the test; supporting grounds are.

options.label: Who first put it forward
options.rationale: The source isn't the test; the grounds are.

questions.explanation: Dewey defined reflective thought as careful consideration of any belief in the light of the grounds that support it.

questions.prompt: Back at the dark café, which question would logic and critical thinking ask?

options.label: Do dark windows really show it is closed?
Is this a café worth visiting?
options.rationale: Taste in cafés isn't the issue; the reasoning is.

options.label: How many people think it is closed?
options.rationale: A headcount isn't a ground for the claim.

options.label: Does the owner seem friendly?
options.rationale: Friendliness has nothing to do with the claim.

questions.explanation: Both ask whether the reason offered (dark windows) really supports the claim (closed).
